title: Blindspots 3 Vimalakirti
speaker: Heigaku Talus Latona
summary: Heigaku Talus Latona takes up the Vimalakirti Sutra and its teaching of non-duality as a way back into the tea lady koan, where decrepit and miraculous are both fully present. Joan Tollifson's description of opposites as inseparable points toward the dissolving of subject and object. Heigaku reads Burton Watson's translation of the scene in which a goddess scatters flowers that fall from the bodhisattvas but stick to Shariputra and the other major disciples, then answers his questions about emancipation by claiming to have seized on nothing. Heigaku closes with Kiku Christina Lerner's image of practice as Vimalakirti's living room, a heart large enough to be a meeting place for all the angels and demons.

sentences.text: So, we've studied this koan in which the tea lady challenges some monks to show their miraculous powers and then demonstrates hers by the everyday act of pouring tea.
We observed that it incorporates concepts we've discussed in Zen of giving and receiving, formalities around who goes first.
We've looked at the concept of pilgrimage and when we put down what we're working on, when we put down awareness and pick it back up.
We noted that Bodhicitta, the desire for awakening, seems to be present in everyone in the story, but some have some blind spots around that.
We've noted some contrasts in the language of the story of the decrepit versus miraculous, the woman describing herself as a decrepit old woman and yet her powers are miraculous.
That decrepit versus miraculous kind of ties into the next concept that I wanted to talk about.
So last week we talked about Bodhicitta, which is one of the Buddhist teachings that receives a much heavier emphasis in the Mahayana school.
Another teaching with elevated emphasis in Mahayana is non-duality.
One of the widely studied Mahayana sutras is the Vimalakirti Sutra.
In a context of exquisite humor, the core teaching of the Vimalakirti Sutra is non-duality.
The teaching of non-duality challenges us to go beyond every observation we make, recognizing that it is not completely true and it is also not false.
There is not a solid line of separation between anything and its opposite.
Knowledge and ignorance, for example, are explored.
We treat them as being two different ideas, but non-duality teaches that they are not two.
To quote the sutra, *the natures of ignorance and knowledge are the same, for ignorance is undefined, incalculable, and beyond the sphere of thought*.
The realization of this is the entrance into non-duality.
We could say the same for decrepit and miraculous.
They are not two; both are strongly present in the story.
Non-duality is not the same as the teaching that all is one, because that one is a single concept.
It's like trying to put myriad experience into a single box.
The ancient literature always refers clearly to not two.
The ultimate nature of reality is without separations.
Separation is an illusion that we project onto experience.
Joan Tollefson summarizes that reality is completely inescapable and thus completely unattainable, for there is nothing apart from it to find it or to lose it.

In response to the question of what is non-duality all about, she replies, *It is the dissolution of every answer to that question, and there is diversity and variation in reality, but not separation.
Opposites are inseparable aspects of one whole.* She has to make that observation of dissolving all answers because no words can adequately describe the non-dual nature of reality.
For example, she uses the word inseparable, but for inseparable to have meaning, there must be separable.
While words cannot answer or explain, they can point.
They can direct us to a path which we can follow, to familiarity with non-duality.
The climax of non-duality is the dissolution of the difference between subject and object, between ourselves and our perceptions.
G.
Show Warner explores an approach to breaking down the mental barrier that separates ourselves from others.
When we interact, we are continuously transmitting information to each other.
The information conveyed in body language and expression has far greater impact than our original intention in speaking.
The ideas transmitted are incorporated in the other person's thought processes.
With the intermingling of our minds, is this my idea or your idea?
How can we be separate?
Carrying this analysis further breaks down the separation between life and death.
If many of the ideas in my mind originated and were transmitted by my grandmother, then the ideas that make up who she is live on after her death.

The Vimalakirti Sutra plowed fresh ground as it spread in the second and third centuries of the common era, with its teachings that not just monastics but also lay practitioners have the potential for great awakening.

The sutra also took Shakyamuni Buddha's understated observation that there is not a difference between the sexes and the capacity for enlightenment, and greatly energized it into an asserted teaching.
In the sutra, many of the familiar disciples of the Buddha have their blind spots illuminated.
Here is a passage from Burton Watson's translation, page 86.

*There was a heavenly being, a goddess, in Vimalakirti's room who, seeing Manjushri and Vimalakirti and hearing them expound the law, proceeded to make herself visible and, taking heavenly flowers, scattered them over the bodhisattvas and major disciples.*
When the flowers touched the bodhisattvas, they all fell to the floor at once.
But when they touched the major disciples, they stuck to them and did not fall off.
The disciples all tried to shake off the flowers through their supernatural powers, but they could not do so.
At that time, the goddess said to Shariputra, *Why try to brush off the flowers?
Such flowers are not in accordance with the law*.
He replied, *That's why I tried to brush them off*.
Note that the wearing of flowers and other personal ornaments was forbidden to members of the Buddhist order.
The goddess said, *Don't say these flowers are not in accordance with the law.
Why?
Because the flowers make no such distinctions.
You, in your thinking, have made up these distinctions.
That's all.
If one who has left the household life to follow the Buddhist law makes such distinctions, that is not in accordance with the law.
One must be without distinctions to be in accordance with the law.
Look at the bodhisattvas.
The flowers do not stick to them because they have already cut off all thought of discriminations.
Just as evil spirits are able to take advantage of a person who is beset by fear,*
*so because you disciples are fearful of the cycle of birth and death, the senses of form, sound, smell, taste and touch are able to take advantage of you.
But once a person has done away with fear, then the five desires that arise from these senses will not be able to get at him.

So long as one has not done away with all such entanglements, the flowers will stick to him, but they will not stick to someone who has eliminated them all.* Shariputra said, *Goddess, have you been staying in this room long?* She replied, *Venerable sir, my stay in this room is about as long as your attainment of emancipation.*
Shariputra said, *So you've been here a long time then*.
The Goddess said, *Venerable sir, how long has your attainment of emancipation been?* Shariputra was silent and did not answer.
The Goddess said, *With your great wisdom, Venerable sir, why do you remain silent?* Shariputra replied, *Emancipation cannot be spoken of in words.
Therefore, I do not know what I can say to you.* The Goddess said, *Words writing all are marks of emancipation.
Why?
Because emancipation is not internal, not external and not in between.*
And words likewise are not internal, nor external, nor in between.
Therefore, Shariputra, you can speak of emancipation without putting words aside.
Why?
Because all things that exist are marks of emancipation.

Shariputra said, *Doesn't emancipation mean putting aside lewdness, anger and stupidity?* The Goddess said, *The Buddha, addressing persons of overbearing arrogance, asserted that one must put aside lewdness, anger and stupidity in order to gain emancipation.
That is all.
If he was addressing those who were free of overbearing arrogance,*
*the Buddha asserted that the nature of lewdness, anger and stupidity is emancipation itself.* Shariputra said, *Excellent, excellent.
Goddess, what have you seized on?
What have you seen into that you speak with such eloquence?* The Goddess replied, *I have seized on nothing, seen into nothing and hence speak with eloquence.
Why?
If one claims to have seized on something or seen into something, then in the light of the Buddha's law, one is being overbearingly arrogant.
In The Hidden Record, the book that we're pulling Koans from,*

Jan Willis summarizes this chapter as being a story about the error of focusing on religious purity and the observance of religious rules rather than on the core of religion and spirituality, which is the good heart.
The events in the sutra take place in the living room of the lay practitioner Vimalakirti.

As the story unfolds, the supernatural powers that come with Vimalakirti's enlightened insight allow him to expand his living room to make room for thousands of disciples, Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, and eventually his parlor gets big enough to include the grounds where the Shakyamuni Buddha was teaching along with his whole audience of tens of thousands of people.
Kiku Christina Lerner, abiding abbess of SFCC city center, has a wonderful teaching about how our practice can be like Vimalakirti's living room.
In practice, our heart is able to expand to be large enough to hold all that arises.
It is a meeting place for all the angels and demons we have come to know so well.
Our heart is big enough to feel all of the pain and joy that lives dish out.
Hold that our heart is doing, doesn't mean grab and carry.
Our heart is not an attic or a basement.
This big heart isn't just a warehouse of junk that we accumulate and stay attached to.
The heart holds the active discussion of our lives with its continuously evolving cast of characters.
By sticking with our practice, with study and retreats, and critically with upright, attentive meditation, we can come to see what we didn't have the capacity for before.
